deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft of the opening of Riemann's 1857 paper 'Beiträge zur Theorie der durch die Gauss'sche Reihe F(α,β,γ,x) darstellbaren Functionen' (and of its self-announcement in the Göttingische gelehrte Anzeigen). The previous and next pages draft the general argument that p and q are single-valued. That argument runs: if y1, y2 are two branches, then p and q, expressed through the Wronskian, are unchanged by monodromy, because numerator and denominator both pick up the factor ad-bc.

(A) Euler's class of equations. Write θ = d/d log x = x d/dx. Riemann considers linear second-order equations in which x occurs in only two 'dimensions':
  (aθ² + bθ + c) y = x^λ (a'θ² + b'θ + c') y.
He recalls Euler's remark that these can be solved by power series whose exponents form an arithmetic progression with difference λ.
[Filled in by me:] Put y = Σ_n C_n x^(μ+nλ). Then
  (aρ_n² + bρ_n + c) C_n = (a'(ρ_n−λ)² + b'(ρ_n−λ) + c') C_{n−1}, with ρ_n = μ + nλ,
and the leading exponent μ satisfies aμ² + bμ + c = 0.

(B) Reduction to λ = 1 and a = a'. Riemann says the general case reduces to this one by taking t = a' x^λ / a as the new variable.
[Filled in by me:] Since θ_x = λ θ_t, the equation becomes
  (θ_t² + (b/(aλ)) θ_t + c/(aλ²)) y = t (θ_t² + (b'/(a'λ)) θ_t + c'/(a'λ²)) y.
This is the normal form in the right column:
  (1−x) θ²y + (b − b'x) θy + (c − c'x) y = 0.

(C) Link to Gauss. Up to a factor common to all terms (a power x^μ), the resulting series are Gauss's hypergeometric series.
[Filled in by me:] Gauss's equation in θ-form is θ(θ+γ−1)F = x(θ+α)(θ+β)F, and y = x^μ F satisfies an equation of the normal form. Riemann adds that expressing the series coefficients by Euler integrals (Beta functions) yields definite-integral representations of y, i.e. Euler's integral.

(D) The three characterising properties of y. He says these follow either from the integral representations or from Cauchy's general existence theorems for differential equations (Comptes rendus):
  1. y varies continuously and stays finite except at x = 0, ∞, 1.
  2. All values (branches) of y at the same x are linear combinations, with constant coefficients, of two of them.
  3. At x = 0, ∞, 1, y splits into two components that behave like x^α, x^α' at 0; like (1/x)^β, (1/x)^β' at ∞; and like (1−x)^0, (1−x)^(1−α−α'−β−β') at 1.

These are the defining properties of Riemann's P-function. The next page begins the converse: any function with these properties satisfies such an equation.

[Check by me:] At x = 0 the indicial equation is r² + br + c = 0, so α + α' = −b. At ∞, y ~ x^ν with ν² + b'ν + c' = 0 and ν = −β, so β + β' = b'. At x = 1 the indicial equation is r(r−1) + (b'−b) r = 0, giving exponents 0 and 1 + b − b' = 1 − α − α' − β − β'. This is the Fuchs relation for three singular points.
errors: Property 3 writes the orders as 'x^α, x^α', 0 und …' without separating the points. The orders at ∞ should be in 1/x, i.e. (1/x)^β and (1/x)^β'. The draft is compressed and ambiguous here.

The non-zero exponent at x = 1 must be 1 − α − α' − β − β' (sum of all six exponents = 1). The transcribed 'c−α'+β'−α−β' is either a misreading or a slip; the sign of β' and the constant are wrong as transcribed.
'unendlich klein von der Ordnung' is loose. The exponents may be zero or negative (exponent 0 at x = 1 means the branch stays finite), so 'of order' would be more accurate.
The reduction t = a' x^λ / a requires a, a' ≠ 0 and λ ≠ 0. This is implicit and unstated.
Property 1 (finite except at the three points) holds for generic exponents; it is stated without qualification. This is harmless.

results.what: Equations (aθ²+bθ+c)y = x^λ(a'θ²+b'θ+c')y have series solutions with exponents in arithmetic progression of step λ
results.modern_name: Frobenius series for equations with two-term recurrence / Euler's hypergeometric-type equations

results.what: Reduction via t = a'x^λ/a to the normal form (1−x)θ²y + (b−b'x)θy + (c−c'x)y = 0, whose solutions are x^μ times Gauss series
results.modern_name: Reduction to the Gauss hypergeometric equation

results.what: Integral representation of y by expressing series coefficients through Euler (Beta) integrals
Characterisation of solutions by: singularities only at 0, 1, ∞; branches linear in two of them; prescribed local exponents at each point
results.modern_name: Riemann P-function / Riemann scheme, Fuchs relation

deep.surprise_reason: This is a working draft of the introduction to Riemann's published 1857 hypergeometric paper and its Anzeige. The Euler reference, the three properties of the P-function and the exponent sum all appear in print. The interest is only in seeing the drafting process.

transcription_corrections: The final exponent at x=1 should read '0 und 1−α−α'−β−β'' (sum of exponents =1), not 'c−α'+β'−α−β'.
'Für den Fall daß a, a' {+die Größen+} und λ=1 sind' likely reads 'Für den Fall, daß a = a' und λ = 1 sind' (i.e. a=a', λ=1).
'von einem allen Gliedern gemeinschaftlichen Factor' is preceded by 'abgesehen' (struck/overwritten): the series are, apart from a common factor, Gauss's hypergeometric series.
Property 3 likely lists orders x^α, x^α' (at 0), (1/x)^β, (1/x)^β' (at ∞), and 0 and the remaining exponent (at 1); the transcription conflates them.
The marginal fragment 'x^α x^α'' at the bottom of the right column appears to be a scratch note of the exponent symbols (written x^α, x^α').
